Hello!
I come here with an idea for a collaborative project. The goal is to formalize the statement that any lean-checked proof would need to fulfill in order for the problem to be considered solved. Currently, it is extremely hard as the literature is scattered and old, and the amount of people that carry this expertise are scarce.

Almost none of the downstream math exists here. I made an attempt a few months ago and there are many scattered open source repositories online from which to vendor material.

It would work in a similar way as the PNT+ project, a standalone repo that could be gradually ported into Mathlib.

One thing to take into account is that 3D Yang Mills is not finished. Continnum limit and Balaban´s UV work are completely unbridged, and unformalized. I am also not sure if a 4D proof is even doable without solving 3D first. Only 2D is complete (And also unformalized).

What are your thoughts on this? I have substantive work that could be ported, but of course the bottleneck is not coding thousands of lines, but to know if the theorems are correct, the definitions are correct, the symbols are correct, and what are the exact dependency tree we need to formalize. That must be the first step.
There was a thread on this recently, but I think it got deleted. ccing @Michael R Douglas who is interested in this read, I think.

Hi! I really hope that Balaban's works be formalized AND understood!
I believe that we should start with the UV stability of YM3, but perhaps incomporating new techniques introduced in the later papers by Balaban and Dimock. I can't say that I understand Balaban's, but I am familiar with Dimock's.

I would advocate for the following design goals:

  1. Not covering several dimensions, and instead a narrow focus on strict adherence to the Jaffe-Witten criteria. Its going to be a huge undertaking, keeping the problem well scoped is essential.
  2. Solution neutrality (OS reconstruction, RG, direct Hamiltonian, etc.)
  3. Proper refusal tests (The massive scalar Gaussian field, the one-dimensional theory, etc)
  4. Full provenance of what criteria was included and why, with proper citations, to establish that the criteria are specified as unbiasedly as possible and not used to favor or exclude any particular solution
  5. Full compatibility with Mathlib and other standard toolchains
    I have a skeleton of a paper that provides a Lean architecture for my vision of what that would look like, if interested.

This is a timely request, to have a vetted formal statement of the Yang-Mills Millennium prize problem. Part of such a statement -- the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms of Euclidean QFT -- is already available in the repos OSforGFF (here on Palomar) and OSreconstruction (work in progress but the axioms are cleanly stated along with the Wightman axioms). These axioms are already hard to satisfy so this should keep prospective solvers busy for a while (but these days who knows?).
I am part of a group formalizing the rest of the YM problem statement and we will announce this soon.
@Moritz Firsching i thought someone in formal conjectures working on this?
Yes, @Samuel Fedida and @Jack McCarthy did a bit of work towards this.
Eh, we didn't really make much progress. We made an initial formalization of the Haag–Kastler axioms, but that's about it.

I will create the repo in a few hours. I think this is a plausible first target.

I think it's possible to write Wightman/OS axioms (or import Michael's), but how do we characterize YM? There are in principle many options, but if we stick to 2, then we would have to go the way with the asymptotics vs perturbation theory.

The difficulty is that every formal identification in the cited literature passes through a regularization route, while the route-independent statements are informal. Nonetheless, I think this can be managed because one structural constraint binds every resolution: the global form of G is distinguished by extended observables, line operators and topological sector data, while bounded local observables on contractible regions can be blind to it, which I believe was established here.

extended objects don't satisfy Wightman/OS. I would be in favor of including them if it were a research project, but that's not faithful to Jaffe-Witten... and there is no established bridge for Euclidean->Minkowski for extended objects.
Extended observables can exist in a Wightman/OS quantum field theory. (So can extended excitations)
No. For example Wilson Loops are extended observables but not smeared fields.
Wilson loops are path-ordered exponentials of gauge fields, and gauge fields do not satisfy Wightman/OS axioms. in what sense do Wilson loops exist in Wightman/OS?

1. JW explicitly allowed for options outside of Wightman/OS: "Existence includes establishing axiomatic properties at least as strong as those cited in Streater & Wightman (1964), Osterwalder & Schrader (1973) and Osterwalder & Schrader (1975)" Note the phrase "at least as strong as." You are incorrect that it is "not faithful to Jaffe-Witten" to include solutions outside of Wightman/OS. They intentionally left the door open.
  2. Wilson loops rigorously exist at finite lattice cutoff and can be compatible with OS positivity, noting carefully that their existence as renormalized continuum operators is extra structure and not a consequence of the Wightman/OS axioms.

So when you say that "extended objects don't satisfy Wightman/OS," its not a counter argument to my original point about the structural constraint because (1) JW explicitly does not require that condition and (2) extended observables and excitations are compatible with Wightman/OS anyway even if it did.

Why care? Well the JW statement is extremely clear that Wightman/OS is not required, so any formal problem statement that requires it is unfaithful, full stop. This isn't a technical aside. I would argue that after decades of the brightest minds attempting Wightman/OS, the actual solution will come from a very clever approach from out of left field that makes the "at least as strong as" crucial. Meaning, if a formal problem statement is accepted by the community that does not leave the door open to these solutions explicitly blessed by JW, then it would actively be building a wall to keep out the actual solution.

If you take "as strong as" literally in terms of implication, your framework must be strong enough to produce pointlike fields. So extended objects would not be enough (for example Haag-Kastler net wouldn't be enough). I do not understand what you mean by "are compatible with".

As I said, if it were a research problem, I would be in favor of including Wilson loops. I would be sincerely interested to extend the OS reconstruction theorem to Wilson loops. I wrote something similar on this Zulip months ago.

If you take a look at the story of Balaban (cited in the official problem description), you will notice that the reason why the development stagnated is not the distinction between pointlike/extended. We first need to understand the UV stability. If you construct Wilson loop correlations in the 4d continuum limit in finite volume, I expect that anyone involved would regard it as a breakthrough.

But that's different from what should be the statement of the problem.
